title: A contest starts in fifteen minutes
description: Practice traffic averages 12 submissions/s. A scheduled contest is expected to peak near 200/s, at about three core-seconds per submission. New judge VMs take minutes to become ready. How should you prepare without compromising isolation or runtime fairness?

options.text: Pre-scale toward the estimated 600 busy cores plus headroom, isolate contest capacity and queues, and buffer excess work visibly.
options.explanation: The calendar gives you time to provision before the burst. A queue absorbs variation, and scoring by submission time avoids penalizing users for judging delay.

options.text: Keep the normal fleet and run many more sandboxes per core until reactive scaling catches up.
options.explanation: Oversubscription makes runtimes less reproducible and adds contention precisely during the contest. Known scheduled demand should be provisioned ahead.

options.text: Judge inside API requests so queued submissions do not need extra storage.
options.explanation: Long-running execution would exhaust request capacity and couple API availability to untrusted workloads.

options.text: Temporarily remove sandbox isolation to reduce CPU use at the peak.
options.explanation: Isolation is non-negotiable for arbitrary submitted code. A predictable capacity spike is not a reason to weaken the execution boundary.
